summary: From the library analogy up: the dictionary ADT, direct-address tables and why they waste space, hash functions (division and multiplication), collisions, chaining with insert at head, load factor α = n/m, and why resizing keeps every operation amortized O(1).
sourceNote: Lecture 11 'Hash Tables' (Mon Sep 28) slides, CLRS 11 intro and 11.1 to 11.3. The library phases, the 42/17/82/37/55/99 trace, the m = 16 and prime 2663 examples, and the k = 123456 multiplication example are Poon's. Book letter counts (spaces not counted) are worked out here.

sections.heading: The big picture: find anything in O(1)

blocks.md: Every structure so far makes you **look** for things. An unsorted array: check every slot, O(n). A sorted array: binary search, O(log n). A **hash table** does better: it computes where a thing lives from its name, and goes straight there. On average that's **O(1)**, no matter how much you store. You already use it daily: a JavaScript `Map` or object, a Python `dict`, Java's `HashMap` are all hash tables.

blocks.md: **Why it matters** Hash tables are probably the most used data structure in real software. Every time a website checks if your username is taken, a browser checks if it already downloaded an image, or your code does `obj[key]`, a hash table answers in constant time. If you understand this chapter, you understand why `map.get(key)` is fast and when it isn't.

sections.heading: The library analogy, phase by phase

blocks.md: Poon builds the whole idea as a story about a librarian with 5 books: *Pride and Prejudice*, *Odyssey*, *The Great Gatsby*, *Dracula* and the *Bible*. She needs three operations: **search** for a book by title, **insert** a book, **delete** a book. Each phase fixes the problem of the last one.

blocks.term: Phase 1: one reserved cubby per book
blocks.body: The library has **1,000 cubbies**, each fits one book. She reserves cubby 0 for *Bible*, cubby 1 for *Dracula*, and so on. To search, she walks straight to that book's cubby. Every operation is instant. But 995 cubbies sit empty forever.

blocks.body: The mayor says she can only have **10 cubbies**. So she invents a **rule** that turns any title into a cubby number: count the letters, keep the last digit (the count **mod 10**). *Bible* has 5 letters → cubby 5. *Odyssey* has 7 → cubby 7. Now 10 cubbies can serve any title. But what if two titles get the same number?

sections.heading: The dictionary ADT: keys and values

blocks.body: An abstract data type for storing **key-value pairs** and finding a value quickly by its key. Poon calls it the 'Library ADT (actually the Dictionary ADT)'. (ADT = what the structure does, not how, from Lecture 2.)

The **key** is the piece of information you look things up by; the **value** is what you want back. Library: key = book title, value = the physical book. A real dictionary: key = word, value = definition. A gradebook: key = student name, value = grade.

rows: remove the pair whose key is k

blocks.title: The three operations
The same ADT in code you already know
blocks.body:
JavaScript:
  const grades = new Map();
  grades.set("Alice", 95);      // insert
  grades.get("Alice");          // search → 95
  grades.delete("Alice");       // delete

Java (Poon's slide):
  Map<String, Integer> grades = new HashMap<>();
  grades.put("Alice", 95);        // hashes "Alice" to find a slot
  int grade = grades.get("Alice");  // hashes "Alice" again to retrieve

blocks.md: **How could we build it?** An array or a linked list of pairs works, but search means scanning: O(n). The rest of the chapter builds something that does all three operations in O(1).

blocks.prompt: In a phone's contact list, what is the key and what is the value?
blocks.answer: Key: the contact's name. Value: their phone number (and other details).

sections.heading: Direct-address tables: the key IS the index

blocks.body: The special case where every key is a small whole number. The universe of possible keys is U = {0, 1, …, 9}. Make an array T with one slot per possible key: **T[k] holds the value for key k**, or null if there isn't one. This is Phase 1 of the library.
**U** is the set of every key that could ever show up. **|U|** is how many there are (set size, 'cardinality'): if A = {1, 2, 3} then |A| = 3. A direct-address table needs an array of size |U|.

blocks.body: We **assume** the hash function sends each key to any of the m slots with equal chance, independently of where other keys went. It's an idealization that lets us do the math on average chain length. Real hash functions only approximate it.

blocks.prompt: A hash function returns a random slot each time it's called. Why is that useless?
blocks.answer: It isn't deterministic: insert(k) might store at slot 3 and search(k) might look at slot 8, so you'd never find anything.

sections.heading: Hashing by division: h(k) = k mod m

blocks.body: **a mod m** is the remainder when a is divided by m. 42 mod 10 = 2 (42 = 4·10 + **2**). 17 mod 10 = 7. 123 mod 16 = 11 (123 = 7·16 + **11**). The answer is always between 0 and m−1, which is exactly the range of slot numbers.
**h(k) = k mod m**, where k is an integer key and m is the table size. The library rule was this with m = 10 and k = number of letters.

blocks.title: Hashing by division, m = 10, no collision handling (the slide trace)

frames.caption: An empty table of m = 10 slots. We'll insert six (key, value) pairs with h(k) = k mod 10 and NO collision handling yet. Only keys are shown.
insert(42, 'a'): h(42) = 42 mod 10 = **2**. Slot 2 is empty, so T[2] = (42, 'a').
insert(17, 'b'): h(17) = 17 mod 10 = **7**. Slot 7 is empty, so T[7] = (17, 'b').
insert(82, 'c'): h(82) = **2**, but T[2] already holds 42. **Collision.** Without a plan, we overwrite it and (42, …) is gone for good.

insert(99, 'f'): h(99) = 99 mod 10 = **9**. Slot 9 is empty, so T[9] = (99, 'f').
Final state: 4 keys survived, but 42 and 17 were silently lost. Phase 2 of the library had the same problem. Chaining fixes it.

blocks.body: **h(k) = ⌊ m · (k·A mod 1) ⌋**, with a constant 0 < A < 1. Three steps: multiply k by A, keep only the **fractional part** (that's what 'mod 1' means: 13.657 → 0.657), multiply by m and round down (⌊ ⌋ = floor). A common choice is A ≈ 0.6180339887, related to the golden ratio.

frames.caption: Three steps. The nice thing: m can be anything, even a power of 2, because the fractional part mixes all the digits of k.
Step 1, multiply by A.
Step 2, 'mod 1': throw away the whole-number part 76207 and keep 0.525…
Step 3, scale to the table and round down. So h(123456) = **525**: slot 525 of 1000.

blocks.body: Each slot T[j] holds a **linked list** (a chain) of all the key-value pairs that hash to j. A collision just makes that chain one node longer. This is the librarian's Phase 3.
A new pair goes at the **front** of its chain: point the new node at the old first node, then make T[j] point at the new node. That's O(1) no matter how long the chain is (no walking to the end).

insert(42, 'a'): h(42) = **2**. Chain 2 is empty, so (42, 'a') becomes its only node.
insert(17, 'b'): h(17) = **7**. Chain 7 is empty, so (17, 'b') becomes its only node.
insert(82, 'c'): h(82) = **2**. Slot 2 already has 42. No overwrite: the new pair goes at the **head** of the chain, and 42 is pushed one step back. T[2] = (82, 'c') → (42, 'a').
insert(37, 'd'): h(37) = **7**. Slot 7 already has 17. No overwrite: the new pair goes at the **head** of the chain, and 17 is pushed one step back. T[7] = (37, 'd') → (17, 'b').
insert(55, 'e'): h(55) = **5**. Chain 5 is empty, so (55, 'e') becomes its only node.
insert(99, 'f'): h(99) = **9**. Chain 9 is empty, so (99, 'f') becomes its only node.
Done. All six pairs are stored; nothing was lost. Chains 2 and 7 have two nodes each, and the newest node is always first.

blocks.title: Appendix: how real HashMaps keep keys unique
blocks.body:
Poon's slides assume insert() is only called with a new key. Java's HashMap instead does:

1. j = h(k)                              O(1)
2. walk chain T[j]; if k is found, replace its value with v    O(α)
3. if k wasn't found, insert (k, v) at the head             O(1)

That's why map.put("Alice", 99) after put("Alice", 95) leaves ONE Alice, with 99.

    j = k % m

    j = k % m

    return None

blocks.title: Runtime of chaining (insert at head)

blocks.body: The average chain length: **α = n / m**, where n = number of pairs stored and m = number of slots. Under simple uniform hashing, a search walks about α nodes, so search and delete are **O(α)**.

blocks.md: **The problem:** α = n/m, and n keeps growing, so with a fixed m, O(α) is really O(n). **The fix:** we control m. When the table gets too full, make it bigger.
blocks.slide: α grows with n… unless we grow m

blocks.body: Pick a fixed limit, like **α_max = 0.75**. When an insert pushes α above it, create a new array of size **2m** and re-insert every pair (their slots change, because h depends on m). Doubling m halves α. The copy costs O(n).

frames.caption: Start with m = 4 empty chains and α_max = 0.75. We'll insert 5, 12, 7, then 20.
insert(5): check first. (n + 1) / m = 1/4 = 0.25. Not above 0.75, so no resize.
j = 5 % 4 = 1. Put 5 at the head of chain 1, and n becomes 1.
insert(12): check first. (n + 1) / m = 2/4 = 0.50. Not above 0.75, so no resize.
j = 12 % 4 = 0. Put 12 at the head of chain 0, and n becomes 2.
insert(7): check first. (n + 1) / m = 3/4 = 0.75. Not above 0.75, so no resize.
j = 7 % 4 = 3. Put 7 at the head of chain 3, and n becomes 3.
insert(20): (n + 1) / m = 4/4 = 1.00. That's above 0.75: this insert would overfill the table.
So call resize(2 * m) = resize(8) BEFORE inserting 20.
Keep the old chains as `old`, make 8 new empty chains, set m = 8. Every key has to be re-hashed, because k % 8 is not k % 4.
Re-insert 12: 12 % 8 = 4 (it was in slot 0 before). Every key is copied once: resize is **O(n)**.
Re-insert 5: 5 % 8 = 5 (it was in slot 1 before). Every key is copied once: resize is **O(n)**.
Re-insert 7: 7 % 8 = 7 (it was in slot 3 before). Every key is copied once: resize is **O(n)**.
Back in insert: j = 20 % 8 = 4, add 20 at the head, n = 4. Now α = 4/8 = 0.50: short chains again.

trace.code:
def insert(k, v):
    global n
    if (n + 1) / m > 0.75:   # too full?
        resize(2 * m)
    j = k % m
    T[j].insert(0, (k, v))   # at head
    n += 1

def resize(new_m):
    global T, m
    old = T
    T = [[] for _ in range(new_m)]
    m = new_m
    for chain in old:
        for (k, v) in chain:
            T[k % m].insert(0, (k, v))

blocks.body: An accounting method: spread the cost of the rare expensive step (the O(n) resize) over all the cheap operations around it. If the **average** cost per operation stays constant, we say the operation is **amortized O(1)**. The librarian 'counts the cost of that copy by spreading a little of it over all the many fast searches'.

blocks.body: Amortized O(1) is not 'every call is O(1)'. One insert can cost O(n) when it triggers a resize; the promise is about the **average over many calls**. And it rests on SUHA: a terrible hash function that sends everything to one slot makes search O(n) no matter how big m is.
